subs.text: You're now standing in front of the Théâtre de l'Odéon.
Look at the left-hand side of the building.
You should see a small commemorative plaque set into the stone.
This plaque is dedicated to Jacques Guierre, an FFI fighter — that's the Forces Françaises de l'Intérieur, the interior resistance forces —
who was killed on this square at the age of 20, on the morning of 25 August 1944.
It's a fitting introduction to what's coming next.
The FFI didn't fight a conventional battle.
Their role during the insurrection was to disrupt the Germans as much as possible —
and crucially, to gather intelligence and pass it to the Allies, so that the French and American armies could enter Paris with some idea of what they were walking into.
Jacques Guierre was barely 20 years old.
He died on this square, on this very morning.
The plaque is the only mark of it.
From here, continue down Rue de l'Odéon, then turn onto Rue Monsieur-le-Prince.
Stop at the corner of Rue Monsieur-le-Prince and Rue de Vaugirard.
Start the audio for stop 3 when you're there.
You're now in front of the Sorbonne's main entrance.
Pay close attention to the right-hand column at the entrance.
The bullet holes are still there.
Liberation-week scars that the university has chosen never to repair.
The Latin Quarter — and the Sorbonne in particular —
became one of the most important pockets of fighting on the Left Bank during the August 1944 insurrection.
Students, FFI fighters, and ordinary Parisians made these streets some of the fiercest battlegrounds of the week.
The bullet holes on this column are a direct reminder of that.
From here, walk around the Sorbonne to the other side of the building.
Find the observatory tower, and start the next audio as soon as you catch sight of it.
